packages.label: נֶפֶשׁ וּמַחֲלֹקֶת — הָרָצוֹן
packages.reason: All four nodes in this package share the essential nature of רָצוֹן (will/desire) as their common denominator. The Rebbe explicitly states: 'נֶפֶשׁ הוּא בְּחִינַת רָצוֹן' (soul is an aspect of will) in the context of Yom Kippur, where 'afflict your souls' means subdue your will. Simultaneously he equates מַחֲלֹקֶת with 'רְצוֹנוֹת אֲחֵרִים שֶׁלֹּא כִּרְצוֹנוֹ' — strife is nothing other than alien wills opposing one's will. The package is marked neutral because the concept of רָצוֹן itself is structurally neutral: it can be one's own holy will (oriented toward God, expressed as נֶפֶשׁ), or the alien wills of others (expressed as מַחֲלֹקֶת). The teaching's central pivot is precisely this identification: fasting subdues the נֶפֶשׁ/רָצוֹן, which thereby annuls the רְצוֹנוֹת אֲחֵרִים/מַחֲלֹקֶת.
merge_notes: Raw Component A {נפש, רצון} (edge ID 2777) and Raw Component B {מחלקת, רצונות אחרים שלא כרצונו} (edge ID 2781) merged on shared nature.

Both components are expressions of the same underlying domain: the nature of רָצוֹן (will). Component A defines the positive pole: soul = will, the inner orientation of the person. Component B defines the negative pole: strife = alien/other wills. These are not cause-and-effect — they are two faces of the same structural reality of 'will'. The Rebbe's entire argument rests on this identification: fasting subdues the נֶפֶשׁ (= רָצוֹן), and this is exactly what nullifies מַחֲלֹקֶת (= רְצוֹנוֹת אֲחֵרִים). Same essential nature, different orientation.

The Zohar passage cited (Acharei 68) confirms the identity: 'תְּעַנּוּ אֶת נַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם' means to subdue the רָצוֹן — both נֶפֶשׁ and מַחֲלֹקֶת are defined in terms of רָצוֹן in the same passage. This shared bechina-definition justifies the merge.

packages.label: צְדָקָה וְתַעֲנִית
packages.reason: These two nodes share the essential nature of the spiritual practice of self-denial and giving from oneself. The Rebbe equates them explicitly via the Talmudic statement (Berakhot 6): 'אַגְרָא דְּתַעֲנִיתָא צִדְקְתָא' — the reward/merit of fasting is charity. He explains: the essential quality of fasting IS charity (צְדָקָה הוּא בְּחִינַת תַּעֲנִית). Both express the same underlying act: withdrawing from self-gratification and redirecting toward a higher good — in fasting, one withholds food from oneself; in charity, one withholds money for oneself and gives to another. Both are the same essential practice of self-transcendence in service of the higher will. The polarity is good because both are positive spiritual practices in the Torah's framework.
